title: Scaling Depot: Solving a thundering herd problem
summary: When upstream systems fail, retries pile up fast and your database becomes the bottleneck. Here's how we used PlanetScale's Insights to identify and fix the queries that were slowing us down during thundering herd events.
body_text: Depot has scaled from tens of individual builds to tens of millions of builds happening every single week across the platform. With that scale comes new feature requests from thousands of new organizations looking to get faster builds. But at that scale, we have to balance developing new features with revisiting previous decisions and systems that aren't as performant and scalable as they used to be. Everything is an iteration that was built for a point in time that was meant to scale to another point. We've been revisiting a lot of these types of systems internally to see where we need to further scale. We're going to make this a regular series on our blog to share the new things we're building and learning as we scale to meet the demand of the thousands of organizations that are trusting us with their builds. The thundering herd This first post in the series focuses on what we call "the thundering herd problem". It arises when upstream systems outside of our control experience issues. These problems cascade downstream and affect our ability to launch runners for GitHub Actions or container image builds. Some examples of where pressure is put on our systems from upstream issues: Capacity issues for Amazon EC2 in a given region or availability zone Region outages that impact the EC2 API GitHub outages that prevent jobs from being delivered down to runners Our system attempts to retry so we can continue to run builds and jobs in a timely manner. But when the upstream problem is ongoing, this demand can build up rather quickly. This growing group of retries and new attempts is what we refer to as the thundering herd. There are multiple facets of the thundering herd that require addressing. The two main ones are: Applying some backpressure into the system to lower demand during these times Ensuring the system has the capacity to handle this higher demand (which will be needed as we scale anyways) This post focuses on handling higher demand, specifically around our database. Handling higher demand During a thundering herd event, what would normally be manageable database traffic suddenly spikes. We've seen CPU usage jump to 100%, which cascades into a much larger problem. Some key components of our system rely on the database, so when it's struggling, the impact to other parts of our system may grow. We use PlanetScale for database management and we use their dashboards and insights to monitor the state of the DB. PlanetScale exposes metrics that help us understand what's happening with our database in real time. When issues arise, we can check the CPU metrics dashboard to see if we're hitting database constraints. Since the database is a critical point of failure, catching these spikes early is essential. The Insights page is particularly valuable. It surfaces: Which queries are consuming the most CPU time Query latency distributions (p50, p95, p99) Queries that are scanning excessive rows Lock contention on specific tables Utilizing metrics exposed during thundering herd events, we're able to quickly identify which queries are contributing the most to load and prioritize optimization work accordingly. Some optimizations we've made Queries without indexes First, we systematically went through all the queries we perform against PlanetScale and looked for the ones without indexes. PlanetScale makes this task easy: those queries are highlighted on the Insights page (indicated by the exclamation point icon). A query that doesn't use an index Not all queries need to use an index. It really depends on the frequency of the invocation, and the volume of data it operates on. It's also a trade-off between latency and memory usage. That being said, we identified all the low hanging fruit and added indexes where it made sense. Optimizing existing indexes PlanetScale has a "Recommendations" page, where among other things, it recommends adding or deleting indexes. Sometimes this page has great recommendations, but those are not always silver bullets. One other good indicator of missing or lacking indexes is taking a look at the Insights page and identifying queries with high p50 (and even p99) latencies. Again, this isn't always possible playing a game of trade-offs, but a good p50 query latency should stay below 100ms. To drill down, one can always run an "EXPLAIN ANALYZE" against the query, or use the "Indexes" tab to see which indexes are being selected for a particular query. When a query is taking more than 1s to run, PlanetScale provides an "Explain" page for the given invocation which reveals an even more detailed breakdown. PlanetScale dashboard Explain page showing the details of a slow query Using these tools, we identified multiple schemas where we could dramatically improve index usage. Notice the drops in latency in the following images that were pasted into the company chat following the deployment: PlanetScale dashboard showing a dramatic drop in query latency PlanetScale dashboard showing another example of a dramatic drop in query latency Query batches While looking at Insights, we noticed that some queries (both selects and updates) that use where id in ? clauses were scanning more rows than expected and had higher latency. Further investigation into the indexes revealed that they were not using the primary key to look up items. We discovered that beyond a certain threshold of items in a where .. in clause, the database would no longer use the primary key efficiently. We ended up batching the items we were looking up into multiple queries so that each look up was much faster. We were able to use the PlanetScale UI to see which index was being used for a particular query and then validate that after the change, it was using the primary key for lookups as expected. We didn’t identify a clear threshold for when to do which pattern and opted for tuning the batch sizes as necessary. We considered the tradeoff between the number of round trips to the database vs. the latency of the responses. Optimizing transaction usage We noticed that some queries run as part of a transaction being aborted. PlanetScale makes it easy to notice this on the query details page: PlanetScale dashboard showing an aborted transaction We found out that PlanetScale has a 20 second transaction timeout hard limit: the transaction needs to be committed or rolled back within this timeframe. We refactored the related code to not do any heavy lifting within the transaction, making the execution time stay well within the 20 second limit. Optimizing a json_extract query We had some interesting findings come from investigating a table that tracks available Amazon EC2 instances ready to handle workloads. This table isn't anywhere near our largest, but PlanetScale's Insights page showed one of its queries had a disproportionately high "% of runtime used" during thundering herd events. This query filters instances by availability zone and other metadata stored in a JSON column. During normal operations, this query performs well. But during certain types of upstream issues such as when specific availability zones lack capacity, the query's selectivity changes dramatically. If one or more availability zones are out of capacity, we end up with more records using a zone that has capacity, resulting in the query having less selective results. What's normally a query examining 50 rows might suddenly examine hundreds. JSON extract query performance: Normal operations vs Capacity issues This query was performing a json_extract on every single row examined by the index, not just the final result set. Under high load with poor selectivity, this meant extracting JSON fields from hundreds of rows per query, and this query was running tens of thousands of times per minute during the high demand period. We added a new composite index that includes the JSON extraction directly in the index definition. MySQL can now evaluate json_extract(...) as part of the index rather than scanning and extracting from every row. Even when selectivity drops during an outage and we're scanning more potential instances, the indexed JSON extraction keeps performance consistent. Conclusion After implementing these optimizations, we recently experienced another upstream capacity outage. This time, while we did see increased CPU load on the database, we avoided the 100% CPU state that previously made it unusable. This meant we could focus our resolution efforts on the upstream capacity issues without fighting cascading database fallout. PlanetScale's dashboards and Insights page were instrumental in this work. Having visibility into query performance, index usage, and resource consumption made it possible to systematically identify and fix bottlenecks. Without that observability, we would have been guessing at which optimizations to prioritize. This is only one part of the optimizations we're making to increase the reliability and scaling of Depot. We're working on more optimization strategies to reduce demand spikes in the first place and handle other issues we've encountered as well. We'll share more about that work in future posts as we continue to make improvements. FAQ How do I optimize MySQL json_extract queries that slow down under load? Create a composite index that includes the JSON extraction directly in the index definition. This lets MySQL evaluate the json_extract as part of the index scan rather than extracting from every row that matches the initial filter. The performance improvement becomes most noticeable when query selectivity drops and you're scanning more rows. Another option is to add a column to represent the part of the json object you're querying against and add that to the index. However, this is not always a trivial change depending on how your data is populated. Why are my PlanetScale transactions being aborted after 20 seconds? PlanetScale enforces a hard 20 second limit on transactions. They must be committed or rolled back within that window or they get aborted. If you're hitting this limit, refactor your code to avoid heavy lifting inside the transaction. Move any expensive operations outside the transaction boundaries so the actual database work completes well under the limit. Should I add indexes to all queries that PlanetScale flags as not using an index? Not necessarily. It depends on how frequently the query runs and how much data it operates on. Indexes trade memory usage for query latency, so adding them everywhere can backfire. Focus on queries with high invocation frequency, large row scans, or p50 latencies above 100ms. The low hanging fruit is usually obvious from the Insights page metrics. How do I know if my index optimizations actually helped during the next thundering herd event? Watch the CPU metrics dashboard during the event—you want to see elevated load without hitting 100%. Also check the specific queries you optimized in the Insights page to confirm their latency distributions (p50, p95, p99) stay consistent even under increased traffic. If you previously hit database CPU limits and this time you didn't, that's your clearest signal the optimizations worked. Related posts 8x faster queries with PlanetScale Metal Kysely dialect for PlanetScale Accelerating builds: Improving EC2 boot time from 4s to 2.8s Knowledge share: Insights from the us-east-1 outage on October 20th Iris Scholten Staff Engineer at Depot Peter Hasko-Nagy Staff Engineer at Depot

body_text: Aardvark Therapeutics to Present at Upcoming Investor Conferences in December November 25, 2025 PDF Version SAN DIEGO, Nov. 25, 2025 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aardvark Therapeutics, Inc. (Aardvark) (Nasdaq: AARD), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing novel, small-molecule therapeutics to activate innate homeostatic pathways for the treatment of metabolic diseases, announced that it will present at the following conferences during December: Piper Sandler 37 th Annual Healthcare Conference in New York Presentation: Wednesday, December 3 at 8:00 a.m. ET Evercore ISI 8 th Annual Healthcare Conference in Miami Presentation: Thursday, December 4 at 11:15 a.m. ET Live webcasts of each presentation will be accessible on the company’s website, www.aardvarktherapeutics.com , under the investors section and an archived recording will be available on the website for approximately one month following each presentation. About Aardvark Therapeutics, Inc. Aardvark is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing novel, small-molecule therapeutics designed to suppress hunger for the treatment of PWS and metabolic diseases. Recognizing hunger (the discomfort from not having eaten recently) is a distinct neural signaling pathway separate from appetite (the reward-seeking, desirability of food). Our programs explore therapeutic applications in hunger associated indications and potential complementary uses with anti-appetite therapies. Our lead compound, oral ARD-101, is in Phase 3 clinical development for the treatment of hyperphagia associated with PWS, a rare disease characterized by insatiable hunger. ARD-101 is also being studied in hypothalamic obesity. Aardvark is also developing ARD-201, a planned fixed-dose combination of ARD-101 with a DPP-4 inhibitor, and conducting two separate trials with a goal of addressing some of the limitations of currently marketed GLP-1 therapies for the treatment of obesity and obesity-related conditions. For more information, visit aardvarktherapeutics.com . title: Garment Manufacturing Made Simple for Designers & Brands
summary: Learn how garment manufacturing works, and see how real brands go from concept to clothing line. Read now and skip the costly mistakes.
body_text: If you’ve tried taking a clothing idea from sketch to store shelves, you know this stage can make or break a collection. Garment manufacturing is the bridge between design and delivery, where precision matters as much as creativity. For new or growing brands, it can feel like a black box filled with acronyms, mismatched quotes, and factory emails that read like a different language. This guide demystifies the process. You’ll learn what actually happens inside a production workflow, what timelines to expect, and how to avoid rookie mistakes that cost time and money. Quick note: AI Techpacks can auto-create factory-ready tech packs—the document manufacturers rely on for measurements, fabrics, trims, and construction. You don’t need software to follow this guide, but if you want fewer sampling errors and faster communication, it helps. What Is Garment Manufacturing? Garment manufacturing is the controlled process of turning a design into a physical product—from finalized specs to finished goods leaving the factory. Think of it as a pipeline of defined stages, each only as strong as the prep that feeds it. Every phase builds on the last. For example, a missing fabric code, vague stitch note, or incomplete measurement can snowball into costly rework. Your most valuable asset before placing a purchase order is a precise, up-to-date tech pack . Production can be domestic or overseas. Domestic often means smaller minimums and faster feedback loops. Overseas (Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe) can offer lower unit costs or specialized machinery. The right choice depends on your budget, category, quality bar, and volumes. So garment manufacturing isn’t just making clothes. It’s coordinated design validation, production planning, and quality execution. Managed well, it turns vision into a consistent, scalable inventory. Managed poorly, it can stall a launch or sink a season. Choose Your Production Model: CMT vs. Full-Package (OEM) Before you sew a single stitch, decide how you’ll work with your factory. Two models cover most scenarios: CMT (Cut–Make–Trim) and Full-Package (OEM). The right choice depends on your experience, bandwidth, and how buttoned-up your specs are. CMT (Cut–Make–Trim) With CMT, you provide the materials, trims, patterns, and a complete tech pack. The factory cuts, sews, and finishes to your specifications. You get tight control over inputs and can insist on exact fabrics or certified components. The trade-off is coordination: you (or your sourcing partner) must order on time, confirm deliveries, and ensure patterns are production-ready. If something’s late or incorrect, the line stalls, and that’s on you. This model is best when you have sourcing experience, repeat styles, or niche materials that you want to control. The upsides are control, flexibility, and often lower factory markups. But watch out for heavier project management, zero cushion for sourcing mistakes, and a higher bar for tech-pack accuracy. Full-Package (OEM) In Full-Package, the factory handles sourcing, patterns, sampling, and bulk production through finishing. You focus on approving designs, fits, and pre-production samples while one partner manages the moving parts. This convenience usually comes with higher unit costs and, unless you negotiate visibility, less transparency into the exact mills or trim suppliers. Use Full-Package when you’re launching your first collection, running a lean team, or prioritizing speed to market. The upsides are one point of contact, fewer handoffs, and a lower risk of gaps between vendors. Just be aware of higher per-unit pricing, possible opacity in sourcing, and MOQs that can skew higher. Hybrid (a practical middle ground) Many brands mix the two. One common example is the factory sources standard trims and labels while you supply a specialty fabric or proprietary zipper. Spell out who supplies what in the purchase order, include lead-time assumptions, and confirm how substitutions are approved. A clear split keeps costs predictable and responsibilities clean. The Garment Manufacturing Process, Step by Step Once you’ve picked a production model, the workflow moves through a predictable sequence. The goal is to turn a concept into a consistent product while reducing rework. Step 1: Tech Pack & Specs Everything starts with a complete tech pack: sketches, measurements, a graded size chart, fabric and trim specs, colorways, stitch types, label artwork, and a bill of materials. Factories use this to quote, plan, and sample. Vague specs multiply sampling rounds and cost. Use AI Techpacks to generate your tech pack and keep measurements, material codes, and revisions consistent so errors don’t reach the sewing line. Step 2: Pattern Making & Grading Pattern makers translate your specs into paper or digital patterns. Once the base size fits correctly, grading scales the pattern across sizes to keep proportions balanced. Good grading prevents odd sleeve lengths, tight necklines, or distorted hems as sizes change. Step 3: Sampling Sampling proves the design and construction before you commit to bulk. You’ll typically see three milestones. Prototype (Proto): Validates style and construction. Fit sample: Dials in measurements and comfort. Pre-production (PP) sample: The reference for bulk. Expect two to three rounds total. Don’t rush approvals; catching a mistake here is far cheaper than fixing it in production. Step 4: Cutting & Sewing After PP approval and materials in-house, the fabric is inspected, spread, and cut per the graded markers. Pieces move through sewing lines set up by operation (collar attach, sleeve join, hemming). Clear work instructions and in-line checks matter here; small errors can magnify quickly on an active line. Step 5: Finishing & Quality Control Finishing covers thread trimming, button or label application, pressing, folding, and packing. Most factories follow a defined quality level, such as AQL 2.5, using statistical sampling to decide pass/fail. Units that pass are poly-bagged or boxed per your packing instructions and prepared for shipment. Step 6: Handoff to Logistics Cartons are sealed, palletized if needed, and transferred to your freight forwarder or the supplier’s logistics partner. This is where Incoterms (for example, FOB, CIF, DDP) define who pays and who carries risk. We’ll break those down shortly. Key takeaway: The process is linear but interdependent. Strong specs and decisive approvals keep the schedule moving; unclear instructions slow every later step. Realistic Timelines (Post Tech-Pack Approval) Even with a great partner, apparel production takes longer than most first-time founders expect. Timelines shift with product complexity, order size, material lead times, and how quickly you review samples. Plan backwards from your launch date and confirm dates with your factory before you announce anything. Sampling (2–6 weeks) After you finalize the tech pack, most factories need about 7–10 days for the first prototype. You’ll review, consolidate feedback, and approve the next round. Complex styles, custom prints, or multiple fit rounds can stretch this phase to four to six weeks. Pro tip : Use a single revision sheet per round. Fragmented feedback slows teams and creates contradictions. Material Sourcing (often in parallel, 1–3 weeks) In Full-Package, the factory sources materials while sampling proceeds. Stock fabrics and trims move fast; custom dyes or prints can take 2–3 weeks or more. In CMT, you’re responsible for deliveries. Add at least a week of buffer for supplier slips or customs delays. Production Slotting (≈1 week) Once the PP sample is approved and all materials are on site, the factory books your line time. Good factories schedule ahead, so lock your slot early, especially around spring and holiday peaks. Bulk Production (4–8 weeks) Most basics run 30–60 days. Simple knits may sit at the low end. Structured jackets, lined dresses, or multi-panel pieces take longer. Ask how many lines (production teams) your order will get; more lines usually mean a faster turn. QC, Packing, and Prep (≈1 week) After sewing, garments move through finishing, inspection (often to AQL 2.5), pressing, folding, labeling, and packing. Don’t rush QA here; catching defects before shipment protects margins and reputation. Transit (varies by mode) Domestic ground: ~2–5 days. International air: ~5–10 days, including clearance. Ocean freight: ~30–45 days port-to-port, plus customs and drayage. Plan for regional holidays such as Chinese New Year (late Jan–Feb) or Diwali (Oct–Nov). Factory closures and port congestion during these windows can push schedules by weeks. Key takeaway: Expect 8–14 weeks for most styles. Build contingency into your plan, make approvals fast and clear, and keep a rolling calendar of factory holidays and shipping cutoffs. MOQs Explained (and How to Start Small) If you’ve ever been quoted “MOQ 300 pcs/style” or something similar, you’ve hit one of the toughest early hurdles. MOQ means Minimum Order Quantity. It isn’t arbitrary; it’s how factories stay efficient and profitable. Why Factories Set MOQs Every new style has fixed setup costs: pattern verification, marker making, machine setup, labor scheduling, and waste planning. Whether a line runs 30 or 300 units, those tasks still happen. Low volumes spread those costs over fewer pieces, so either the unit price rises sharply or the factory asks for a higher minimum. MOQs also reflect upstream realities. Fabric and trim minimums: Mills sell by the roll; zipper and label vendors prefer bulk. Line efficiency: Longer, continuous runs keep teams productive and reduce changeovers. Typical Ranges (ballparks) These vary by product and region, but here’s a useful lens. Basics (tees, hoodies): 100–300 units per style/color Denim & outerwear: 200–500 units Swim/lingerie: 100–200 units Luxury or bespoke ateliers: 25–100 units Domestic shops (U.S./Canada) often accept lower MOQs at a higher per-unit price, which can still make sense for first runs. How To Start Small Without Burning Bridges Focus your line: Launch with one to three core styles instead of ten. Use color variations to meet fabric minimums without exploding SKUs. Choose stock materials: Ask for in-stock fabrics and trims. You avoid mill minimums and shave weeks off sourcing. Request a pilot run: Be upfront that you’re testing market fit. Some factories will take 50–100 units if you pay a development fee or accept a slightly higher unit price. Go small-batch or local: Regional factories are built for shorter runs and quick feedback loops. Yes, it costs more per unit, but you’ll learn faster and avoid dead inventory. Consolidate components: Standardize buttons, labels, or linings across styles to hit supplier minimums sooner. Mind your markers: Efficient size and color splits (e.g., S–XL in a tight distribution) reduce fabric waste and keep the cost-per-unit in check at lower volumes. Pro tip : Treat the first PO as a product and relationship test. Clean tech packs, consolidated feedback, and on-time payments make factories far more flexible the next time you ask for a small run. Quality Control 101 (AQL, Inspections, Tolerances) Great design won’t save a collection if quality slips. In apparel, quality control isn’t a final checkpoint; it’s a thread that runs from your first spec to the last packed carton. Whether you’re making 50 or 5,000 units, setting clear standards protects margins and brand trust. Why QC Matters Factories juggle many orders at once. Without clear expectations, issues creep in like uneven stitching, skewed prints, off-size measurements, and missing trims. These aren’t minor annoyances. They drive returns, rework, and reputation damage. Bake QC into every step and you’ll ship more consistent products with fewer headaches. AQL (Acceptable Quality Limit) Most factories and inspection agencies use AQL based on ISO 2859 sampling. You select a quality level that defines how many defects are acceptable in a sampled lot before the shipment fails. For everyday apparel, AQL 2.5 is common. Premium products may use AQL 1.5 or 1.0. Stricter levels reduce defect tolerance but can add time and cost. Choose the tightest standard your price point can support, then apply it consistently. The Inspection Moments That Matter Pre-Production (PPI): Verify fabrics, trims, and critical specs before sewing starts. Catching a bad dye lot here saves a re-cut later. In-Line (DUPRO): Inspect while the line is running. This is where you stop problems from multiplying. Pre-Shipment (PSI) / Final Random (FRI): Sample packed goods against your AQL before they leave the factory. Use this as a release gate for payment and handoff. You don’t need all three on every order, but at a minimum, use an in-line or pre-shipment inspection on new styles or new factories. Tolerances Measurements need tolerances (the acceptable plus/minus range) so teams know what’s “within spec.” For example, chest width 50 cm ± 1.0 cm or sleeve length 62 cm ± 0.5 cm. Without tolerances, good units get rejected or inconsistent ones slip through. Add tolerances to the size chart in your tech pack and ensure the factory’s QC sheet mirrors them. Make QC Actionable Document it in the PO: State your AQL level, which inspection(s) you’ll use, and the pass/fail criteria. Share golden samples: Keep a signed PP sample in your office and require the factory to keep one on the line. All approvals reference these. Define defect classes: Minor, major, and critical defects shouldn’t be guesswork. Spell out examples so inspectors align with your standards. Close the loop: When issues appear, update the tech pack or work instructions, not just the email thread. Pro tip : If you’re new, hire a third-party inspector for the first one or two orders. The report doubles as a training tool for you and the factory. Labels & Compliance for the U.S. Market If you sell in the U.S., labeling isn’t optional. The FTC and CPSC set rules that apply to everyone—from indie brands to big-box suppliers. Miss them and you risk fines, shipment holds, or forced relabeling. The good news is that once you set up a clean system, compliance becomes routine. Four Things Every Garment Must Disclose Fiber content: List fibers in order of predominance (e.g., 95% Cotton, 5% Spandex). Country of origin: Where the garment was made (cut and sewn), not where the fabric came from. Manufacturer or RN: You can use your company name or an FTC-issued RN (Registered Identification Number). Care instructions: Provide at least one safe cleaning method and any relevant temperature or cycle guidance. These requirements stem from the Textile and Wool Acts and the Care Labeling Rule. If you use care symbols, include text somewhere (label or hang tag) so customers don’t guess. Placement and Permanence Labels should be durable and easy to find at the point of sale. For tops, place the identity and fiber/COO label at the center of the back neck. For bottoms, inside the waistband or side seam is good. Care info can sit on a separate label. If a garment has detachable parts (e.g., a liner), each piece may need its own label. Heat transfers are fine if they remain legible for the life of the garment. Care Labeling Rule, in Practice Give customers instructions they can follow at home or with a cleaner without damaging the item. At minimum, specify a safe method (machine wash, hand wash, or dry clean). Add what matters: water temperature, cycle type, drying, ironing, and don’ts such as “Do not bleach” or “Do not iron decoration.” If a process is required for safe cleaning, say so (e.g, “Dry clean, petroleum solvent only”). Children’s Apparel: CPSIA Extras For products sized for 12 and under, you’ll need tracking labels (batch or date codes) and compliance certificates covering applicable standards (lead content, flammability, small parts where relevant). Keep test reports and certificates organized; customs can request them. Make Compliance Foolproof Centralize specs: Keep label copy, RN, care icons/text, and placement notes in your tech pack. Lock artwork: Provide print-ready files for size tabs, brand labels, and care labels so factories don’t “recreate” art. Sample the label: Approve label content and placement on the PP sample and photograph it for the record. Audit occasionally: Spot-check production to ensure label text, RN, and COO match the PO and style. Pro tip : Build a one-page “Labeling Matrix” that lists each style, material variations, and the exact label set it should receive. Share it with the factory’s trim room and QC team. It prevents mix-ups and speeds inspections. Shipping Terms (FOB, CIF, DDP) When cartons are sealed, your last big decision is how risk and cost move from the factory to you. Incoterms (International Commercial Terms) spell this out. You don’t need all 11. For most apparel shipments, learn these three and you’ll avoid surprises. FOB — Free On Board Under FOB, the supplier’s responsibility ends once goods are loaded on the vessel at the origin port. From that point, you own the freight, insurance, risk, and customs. This is good for brands with a freight forwarder or import experience. You control carriers, routes, and costs; pricing is transparent. But there’s a trade-off: you manage more steps and handle any post-departure hiccups. CIF — Cost, Insurance, and Freight With CIF, the supplier pays for ocean freight and basic insurance to the destination port. You take over after arrival: customs, duties, local delivery. This is good for teams that want fewer moving parts but still manage import clearance. And there’s less coordination on the origin-side freight. Trade-offs are limited visibility into rates and schedules; supplier markups are common. DDP — Delivered Duty Paid DDP is the all-in option. The supplier handles everything—freight, insurance, customs, duties, and delivery to your door for a single price. It’s good for new importers or lean teams, and offers simplicity and predictable invoices. The trade-offs are a higher total cost and less control over how customs is handled. Picking the Right Term Cost visibility: If you need to compare landed costs across styles or seasons, FOB gives cleaner numbers. Team capacity: If you don’t have a forwarder or import broker, DDP removes the heavy lifting. Cash flow: CIF and DDP can feel easier, but watch for embedded margins. Ask for a freight cost breakdown before you agree. Country risks and holidays: Ports back up around peak seasons and holidays. Whatever term you choose, build buffer time into your delivery promise. Put your chosen Incoterm, named place (e.g., “FOB Shanghai”), and who books insurance in writing on the PO. Don’t rely on phrases like “shipping included.” That could mean CIF, DDP, or even EXW (factory door pickup), which pushes almost everything to you. Pro tip : Even on DDP, request copies of the commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading/airway bill, and duty/tax proof. You’ll need them for landed-cost analysis and future planning. Conclusion Garment manufacturing is a sequence. When your specs are clear, approvals are decisive, and roles are defined, the process moves. Most delays trace back to fuzzy tech packs, late materials, or slow feedback. Fix those three and you’ll feel the schedule click into place. If you want to reduce sampling errors and keep all details synced, you can use AI Techpacks to generate your tech packs automatically . It will keep your measurements, BOMs, and revisions organized so factories can execute faster. 學習方式、互動深度與適用對象 三個角度出發，幫你快速看出哪款更符合自己的需求。 Toko vs Speak：對話自由度 vs 結構化帶練 Toko 對話很像真實聊天，當下就能把詞語儲存並運用，講完立刻拿到更地道的說法。 Speak 按課綱走，適合從零打底與習慣固定節奏的人。 📖 延伸閱讀： tokotutor.com/blog/toko-vs-speak Toko vs TalkMe：自然表達改善 vs 細節評分發音 Toko 更強調在對話裡即時改寫與延伸，讓你習慣「用英文思考再說出來」。 TalkMe 的發音評分與考試題型很完整，適合想看分數與準備考試的人。 📖 延伸閱讀： tokotutor.com/blog/talkme-vs-toko Toko vs ePOP：口說輸出 vs 題庫打底 想真正「 練習英文 」而不只是背誦？Toko 的多輪情境對話能讓你在真實情境中 開口說英文 、練出自然語感。 ePOP 用題組與聯賽維持動機，對入門與累積字彙文法很有效。 📖 延伸閱讀： tokotutor.com/blog/epop-vs-toko 快速抉擇清單：5 題決策樹找到你的 App 你最卡的是「不敢開口」或「說得不自然」嗎？→ Toko 你需要明確的課綱與真人教學影片嗎？→ Speak 你想看發音/韻律/重音等分數，或同時練多語？→ TalkMe 你目前要先補字彙/文法基礎、喜歡闖關成就感？→ ePOP 你想要 App 會「記住錯誤」並生成專屬練習？→ Toko 📌 常見問題（FAQ） Q1：最好的英文口說學習 App 是哪一個？ 若你的目標是能開口、講得自然、要句級即時糾正與替代表達，我會優先推薦 Toko 。完全初學者需要課綱與教學影片，選 Speak ；在意發音分數或考試導向，選 TalkMe 。 多數使用者實測後的回饋是： Toko 幫助他們「從會背句子，變成敢開口講」，提供的 即時修正與持續回饋機制 。 像 Toko 這類設計完善的 AI App，會在你開口的瞬間標出用字或語法錯誤，並立即提供自然的替代表達。 這比起「事後看解說影片」更有效，因為錯誤當下就被矯正，能直接轉化成語感。 若每天開口練 10–15 分鐘，持續三週以上，你會發現不再需要先在腦中翻譯句子再開口。 這就是 AI 訓練「口語肌肉記憶」的威力。 Q2：哪款 AI App 的發音評分最精準？ 若以「聲學精度」來看， TalkMe 和 ePoP 最細緻，會針對發音、韻律、重音逐一打分。但若你想整句聽起來更自然， Toko 的句級回饋與替代表達更有實戰價值（把分數轉成可用語感）。Toko 支援「母語者會怎麼說這句」，並附上地道替代語，讓你不只是發音正確，而是講得像真的在對話。 Q3：怕開口怎麼練？有沒有「不會有壓力」的英文口說 App？ 有，而且這是許多人選擇 英文口說 App 的原因。Toko 的對話節奏像聊天，錯誤被柔性引導與改敘，不會中斷或扣分，能有效降低語言焦慮，讓你「從敢講開始」。 怎麼練最有效： 先選你最熟的日常或職場話題，連續 7 天，每天 10 - 15 分鐘。 卡住時用提示或中翻英，把同那句話練成更自然說法。 練完後去重播整段對話，記 2–3 個自己常犯的錯，隔天重複。三週後自然度會明顯提升。 Q5：哪款 AI App 最適合上班族或工程師練習英文？ 對職場英文會話、 工程師英文簡報 或 主管英文溝通 有需求的人，Toko 提供的 公司英文主題系列 特別實用。它能模擬開會、報告、提案與跨國協作的情境，讓你不只學單字，而是直接練會說。完全新鮮人可先用 Speak 打底，再過渡到自由對話。 Q6：哪個英文口說 App 會記住我的錯誤，並自動安排專屬練習？ 目前能做到「記錄錯誤+個人化複習」的英文口說 App 仍不多，而 Toko 是其中設計最完整的一款。 Toko 的 AI 會在你練習對話時自動標記錯誤句子與常見用詞，並在之後的練習中主動生成「專屬複習題」與「延伸練習對話」，讓你在不同情境中重複用到那些曾說錯的句子。這種做法能把錯誤轉化為真正的語言輸出記憶，比單純糾正發音或打分更有效。 若你想讓 AI 真正了解你、幫你設計持續可練的內容，Toko 的「專屬複習機制」會是目前最接近真人教練邏輯的設計。 總結：到底哪款英文口說學習 App 最好？ 學 英文口說 最有效的方法，不是背單字，而是每天進行 英文練習 。像 Toko 這類 AI App，能讓你持續開口說英文、累積自然表達力，並讓 AI 幫你修正錯誤、建立語感。 2025 年最推薦的英文口說學習 App： Toko ：最佳整體體驗，強調自然對話、即時糾正與專屬練習。 Speak ：適合初學者，結構清晰、按表操課。 TalkMe ：針對發音與考試題型設計，多數據評分。 ePOP ：遊戲化學習，幫助累積字彙與文法。 所以如果要選一款 最能幫助你持續開口、講得自然又不怕錯 的 App，我會給 Toko 第一名。它的 AI 對話像聊天一樣自然，會根據你說的內容即時糾正、給替代表達，還能回放整段對話讓你看到進步，這種「練得起來」的體驗，是其他 App 難以取代的。 對完全初學者來說， Speak title: How the Atlas 200 Optimizes PlayStation Sound (Tempest 3D Audio on PS5)
summary: How the Turtle Beach Atlas 200 headset optimizes PS5 Tempest 3D Audio for immersive gaming. Setup guide, features & competitive advantages.
body_text: Gaming audio has evolved dramatically, and nowhere is this more evident than with the PlayStation 5's revolutionary Tempest 3D Audio technology. This object-based audio engine simulates sound around you by running an accelerated algorithm that can emulate localized and distant noises from hundreds of sources from a 360-degree range. For gamers seeking the ultimate PlayStation experience, the Turtle Beach Atlas 200 headset stands as the perfect gateway to unlock this immersive audio revolution. What is Tempest 3D Audio on PS5? The Tempest Engine is Sony's dedicated audio processing technology that drives the PS5's 3D audio capabilities. Based on AMD graphics processing technology, the Tempest Engine is a re-engineered AMD GPU compute unit that processes huge amounts of sounds from different sources in game environments. Unlike traditional surround sound that relies on channel-based audio, Tempest 3D Audio creates fully immersive soundscapes where sounds appear to come from all around you. The biggest advantage of having a dedicated audio engine built into the PS5 is eliminating reliance on TV or soundbar audio technologies. Sony researched various ear shapes and sizes using microphones and 22 individual speakers to develop Head Related Transfer Function (HRTF) profiles, ensuring personalized 3D audio experiences for different users. Key Features of the Turtle Beach Atlas 200 The Atlas 200 represents Turtle Beach's first officially licensed PlayStation headset, designed specifically to optimize PS5's advanced audio capabilities through carefully engineered features. 50mm Nanoclear Drivers : High-quality drivers optimized for PlayStation's audio processing, ensuring crystal-clear reproduction of game audio and chat communications while working seamlessly with the PS5's Tempest Engine. Flip-to-Mute Microphone : Intuitive microphone design - flip forward to activate voice chat or flip backward to instantly mute. Simple yet effective for maintaining team coordination during gaming sessions. Lightweight Comfort : Weighing approximately 280g, the Atlas 200 features a floating headband design and memory foam ear cushions for extended gaming sessions without fatigue. How the Atlas 200 Optimizes PS5 Sound The Atlas 200's optimization stems from its integration with Sony's Tempest 3D Audio system. You'll experience 3D Audio through the headphones you already own, either via USB connection to the console or by plugging into the DualSense controller's 3.5mm jack. Seamless 3.5mm Connectivity : Direct connection to the DualSense controller provides immediate Tempest 3D Audio access without additional setup complexity. This wired connection ensures near-zero latency (under 2ms) and uncompressed audio quality. Enhanced Spatial Awareness : The Atlas 200's precise drivers translate PS5's 3D audio processing into clear positional information, allowing players to locate enemies, objectives, and environmental cues with remarkable accuracy in games like Fortnite or Call of Duty. Atlas 200 Headset View Product Comfort and Design for Long Gaming Sessions Extended gaming demands exceptional comfort. The Atlas 200 delivers through lightweight construction and ergonomic design that prevents fatigue during competitive matches. Memory foam ear cushions adapt to individual head shapes, creating comfortable seals that enhance audio isolation. The adjustable headband accommodates various head sizes while distributing weight evenly, eliminating pressure points during extended use. Setting Up Tempest 3D Audio with Atlas 200 Configuring your Atlas 200 for optimal Tempest 3D Audio involves specific PS5 settings adjustments: Navigate to Settings >> Sound >> Audio Output >> Output Device Select "Headset Connected To Controller" for Output Device Set "Output To Headphones" to "All Audio" Access Settings >> Sound >> Volume >> Headphones Set "Volume Control (Headphones)" level to Maximum Adjust microphone levels through Settings >> Sound >> Microphone >> Adjust Mic Level Enable 3D Audio by accessing Settings > Sound and running the setup under 3D Audio for Headphones. The PS5 offers customizable audio profiles tailored to individual hearing characteristics for optimal immersive sound. Benefits of 3D Audio in Gaming Immersion The integration of Tempest 3D Audio technology with the Atlas 200 headset transforms gaming from a visual-focused experience into a truly multi-sensory immersion. Enhanced directionality allows players to pinpoint explosions, gunfire, and player footfalls in multiplayer matches with remarkable precision. Competitive Gaming Context : Wired headsets offer near-zero latency (under 2ms) compared to wireless alternatives that typically achieve 10-25ms in premium models. While latency below 40ms is generally considered excellent for gaming, competitive players often prefer wired connections to eliminate any possible delay, especially in fast-paced games where audio cues can determine victory. Environmental Awareness : 3D spatial audio helps anchor environmental objects and provides persistent presence to targets, making it easier to locate objectives and navigate complex game environments without wandering aimlessly. Narrative Enhancement : When exploring detailed environments, 3D audio helps players locate distant machines or hear subtle environmental details that bring virtual worlds to life, creating what researchers call "presence" - the feeling of actually existing within the game world. For gamers seeking comprehensive gaming setups, Turtle Beach offers additional peripherals like the Stealth 700 Gen 3 wireless headset for those preferring wireless convenience, or the ultra-lightweight Atlas Air for extended comfort. Comparing the Atlas 200 to Other PS5 Headsets The gaming headset market offers numerous options for PlayStation 5 compatibility, yet the Atlas 200 distinguishes itself through official PlayStation licensing and Tempest 3D Audio compatibility at an accessible price point. Wired vs Wireless Performance : While wireless headsets like the Stealth 700 Gen 3 offer convenience, the Atlas 200's wired design provides consistent, near-zero latency audio crucial for competitive gaming scenarios where every millisecond matters. Official PlayStation Licensing : The Atlas 200 represents Turtle Beach's first officially licensed headset for PlayStation consoles, ensuring guaranteed compatibility and optimized performance with Sony's Tempest 3D Audio technology. Value Proposition : The Atlas 200 delivers premium PlayStation audio compatibility at an accessible $59.99 price point, making advanced 3D audio technology available to a broader gaming audience without compromising on audio quality. title: CAS Number Chaos: Why Chemical Lookups Are Harder Than They Look
summary: Why simple chemical lookups are actually complex and how to solve it.
body_text: "Just look up the CAS number." If you've ever worked in chemical sales, you've heard this phrase a thousand times. It sounds simple—every chemical has a unique identifier, right? Just match the number and you're done. Here's the reality: CAS number lookups are one of the most deceptively complex problems in chemical distribution. What seems like a straightforward database query is actually a maze of synonyms, trade names, regional variations, mixture ambiguities, and specification mismatches that breaks traditional automation systems. Let's dive into why this "simple" problem has stumped enterprise software for decades—and what it takes to actually solve it. The Myth of the Universal Identifier The CAS Registry Number system, maintained by the Chemical Abstracts Service, assigns unique identifiers to every chemical substance. In theory, this should make lookups trivial. In practice, it creates as many problems as it solves. Anatomy of a CAS Number 67-64-1 67 Registry group 64 Sequence number 1 Check digit This is Acetone. Simple enough—until your customer calls it "dimethyl ketone," "propan-2-one," or "β-ketopropane." The problem isn't the CAS system itself. It's that customers don't speak in CAS numbers . They speak in trade names, abbreviations, regional conventions, and informal references that vary wildly across industries, geographies, and even individual companies. The Seven Layers of Chemical Identification Hell Through processing millions of RFQs, we've identified seven distinct categories of lookup complexity. Any one of these can break a traditional rules-based system. 1 Synonym Explosion A single chemical can have dozens of valid names. Ethanol alone has 50+ synonyms in common use. CAS 64-17-5 → Ethanol, Ethyl Alcohol, Grain Alcohol, EtOH, Alcohol, Methylcarbinol, Spirits of Wine... 2 Trade Name Chaos Manufacturers create proprietary names that don't reference the underlying chemistry at all. Customer asks: "Tween 80" Also known as: Polysorbate 80, Polyoxyethylene sorbitan monooleate CAS: 9005-65-6 3 Regional Naming Conventions The same chemical has different standard names in different markets. US Aluminum UK/EU Aluminium Same CAS 7429-90-5 4 Isomer & Stereochemistry Confusion Same molecular formula, different structures—and critically different CAS numbers. D-Glucose 50-99-7 L-Glucose 921-60-8 Customer says "glucose" — which one do they mean? 5 Mixture & Blend Ambiguity Many products are blends with no single CAS number. Components may be listed separately or as a mixture. Request: "Denatured Alcohol SDA 40B" This is a blend of Ethanol (64-17-5) + Denatonium Benzoate (3734-33-6) + tert-Butyl Alcohol (75-65-0) in specific ratios. No single CAS exists. 6 Grade & Specification Overload Same CAS number, wildly different products depending on purity, grade, and application. Sodium Hydroxide CAS 1310-73-2 • Technical Grade (95%) • ACS Reagent (97%+) • Food Grade (FCC) • Semiconductor Grade (99.99%) 7 Typos, OCR Errors & Human Mistakes Real-world requests come from scanned PDFs, handwritten notes, and hurried emails. Received: "Sodium Hyrdroxide" (typo) Received: "CAS 67-63-O" (OCR: O vs 0) Received: "Acitone" (misspelling) "A single RFQ can hit three or four of these problems at once. "Need 500kg of the Tween we bought last year, food grade" involves trade names, specification matching, AND historical context." Why Traditional Systems Fail Most chemical distribution software handles identification through lookup tables: massive databases mapping synonyms to CAS numbers, trade names to products, and specifications to SKUs. The Lookup Table Problem Lookup tables sound logical, but they fail in predictable ways: Maintenance nightmare: New trade names appear constantly. Your table is always out of date. Combinatorial explosion: Synonym × Grade × Region × Packaging creates millions of potential mappings. No fuzzy matching: "Sodium Hyrdroxide" returns nothing. The customer waits while someone manually fixes it. Zero context: Tables can't consider "what did this customer order before?" or "what industry are they in?" We've seen companies with 50,000+ row synonym tables that still fail on 30% of incoming requests. Every failure means manual intervention, delays, and frustrated customers. How AI Changes the Game Large Language Models approach chemical identification completely differently. Instead of looking up exact matches in a table, they understand chemicals the way a trained chemist would. Traditional Lookup Exact string matching only Requires pre-built synonym tables Fails on typos and OCR errors No contextual understanding Can't infer missing information Query: "Tween 80 food grade" Result: ❌ NO MATCH FOUND AI-Native Identification Semantic understanding of chemistry Handles synonyms, trade names inherently Robust to typos and OCR artifacts Considers customer history & context Infers grade from application context Query: "Tween 80 food grade" Result: ✓ SKU-PS80-FG (Polysorbate 80, FCC) Chemical Knowledge Built-In LLMs are trained on chemical literature, MSDS documents, and technical specifications. They know that Tween 80 is Polysorbate 80 without needing a lookup table. Fuzzy Matching by Default AI doesn't need exact matches. "Sodium Hyrdroxide" is obviously Sodium Hydroxide. "CAS 67-63-O" is clearly 67-63-0. The model handles these automatically. Contextual Reasoning When a pharmaceutical customer asks for "alcohol," the AI knows to suggest pharmaceutical-grade ethanol, not industrial denatured alcohol—even without explicit specification. A Real Example: The Five-Chemical RFQ Here's a real (anonymized) request that came through our system: Incoming RFQ (PDF attachment, OCR'd) Hi, Please quote the following for delivery to our Newark facility: 200kg MEK (same spec as last order) 500L IPA 99% - electronic grade 50 drums Dowanol PM NMP - pharma grade, need COA 2000kg Methly Ethyl Ketone Thanks, Jennifer A traditional system sees five line items and fails on almost all of them: Request Challenge AI Resolution MEK (same as last) Abbreviation + historical reference → Methyl Ethyl Ketone, Tech Grade (matched to order #4521) IPA 99% electronic Abbreviation + grade inference → Isopropyl Alcohol, Electronic Grade 99% Dowanol PM Trade name (Dow Chemical) → Propylene Glycol Methyl Ether (CAS 107-98-2) NMP pharma grade Abbreviation + regulatory requirement → N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone, USP/NF Grade + COA flag Methly Ethyl Ketone Typo + duplicate detection → Duplicate of line 1, flagged for confirmation Notice the last line: The customer accidentally ordered MEK twice with different names (one abbreviated, one misspelled). Our AI catches this and flags it for human review rather than creating a duplicate order. Building for Chemical Complexity Getting AI to handle chemical identification reliably requires more than just throwing an LLM at the problem. Here's what we've learned building our system: Ground in Your Catalog The AI must be grounded in your specific inventory. It's not enough to identify "Polysorbate 80"—it needs to know you stock three grades and which warehouse has availability. Learn from Your History Historical quotes are gold. When the AI sees how your team has matched vague requests to specific SKUs before, it learns your company's conventions. Human Verification for Edge Cases Some ambiguities genuinely require human judgment. Is "alcohol" ethanol or isopropanol? The AI should flag uncertainty, not guess. The Bottom Line Chemical identification looks like a solved problem from the outside. Just look up the CAS number, right? But anyone who's actually processed RFQs knows the reality: it's a tangled mess of synonyms, trade names, regional conventions, and human error that breaks traditional automation. The companies still relying on lookup tables are leaving money on the table—and leaving customers waiting while their sales teams manually decode requests. AI doesn't just handle this complexity; it handles it instantly, at scale, without maintaining million-row synonym databases. "The question isn't whether AI can handle chemical identification. It's how much longer you're willing to do it the hard way."

title: Not Ready? Why Delaying Customer Onboarding Software Hurts
summary: “Not ready” is usually risk aversion in disguise. This post shows why delaying customer onboarding software quietly increases TTV, adds manual work, and hurts retention. You’ll get a 10-day onboarding playbook, the core KPIs to track (TTV, DTL, capacity), and practical automation moves to go live quickly without ...
body_text: Not Ready? Why Delaying Customer Onboarding Software Costs You (and How to Start Fast) Teams say: “We know we need this, but we’re not ready.” ‍ Translation: risk feels higher than reward. In customer onboarding , waiting compounds cost—slower time to value (TTV) , missed milestones, and frustrated buyers. This guide shows why delaying a customer onboarding platform backfires and gives you a 10-day onboarding playbook to go live fast without breaking your process. Why Waiting on Customer Onboarding Hurts TTV and Retention “Not ready” usually hides risk aversion, not lack of need. While you wait: Momentum dies. New customers disengage when value is slow. Manual work multiplies. Spreadsheets and one-offs don’t scale. Visibility disappears. Execs and buyers can’t see owners, deadlines, or blockers. Churn creeps in. Poor early experiences echo into adoption, expansion, and renewal. A Quick-Start Onboarding Playbook (Live in 10 Days) You don’t need a six-month program. Ship “imperfect but live,” then iterate. Day 1–2 — Define scope + first value Pick one segment/SKU. Write the single “first-value” event (what customers actually care about). Baseline current TTV and DTL. Day 3–4 — Build the customer onboarding playbook 8–12 standardized steps from kickoff → first value. Assign owners + SLAs. No bespoke checklists in the pilot. Day 5 — Stand up an onboarding portal Give customers a clean, no-login view of status, owners, and next steps. This alone reduces anxiety and back-and-forth. Day 6–7 — Turn on onboarding automation Auto-create projects from CRM, auto-assign tasks, set automated reminders. Keep humans focused on change management. Day 8 — Instrument feedback Two pulses: post-kickoff (expectations set?) and post-launch (value achieved?). Day 9–10 — Run two customers and review Publish a weekly scorecard. Fix the top two bottlenecks. Rerun. Must-Track Onboarding KPIs: TTV, DTL, Capacity Time to First Value (TTV): median and p75. Days to Launch (DTL): the speed to go-live. Onboarding Capacity/Throughput: in-flight per CSM and go-lives per CSM. Activation Rate: % hitting first value within target window. Risk Rate: % slipping >7 days with a named blocker. How Onboarding Automation Improves Scale and Visibility Fewer handoffs: CRM → project auto-creation. Consistency: templates + variables = flexible without chaos. Real-time visibility: internal and customer-facing status in one place. Focus time: automation handles nudges; CSMs handle strategy and change. “We’re Not Ready” → Safer Ways to Start (With Guardrails) Scope ruthlessly: one product tier + one segment. Freeze variable work: use playbook variables, not custom checklists. Single source of truth: CRM + onboarding hub + customer view. Sunset parallel trackers. Weekly scorecard: TTV, DTL, capacity, activation, risk. Trigger Events That Mean “Do It Now,” Not Later New funding or headcount ramp Rising enterprise deal mix or longer implementations CRM/ERP migration Compliance or audit pressure Competitors promising faster time-to-insight The Business Case in One Page Revenue: Faster launches pull forward recognition and expansion. Cost: Standardization + automation eliminate rework and status churn. Experience: An onboarding portal reduces buyer’s remorse and boosts advocacy. A 10-Day Starter Checklist (Copy/Paste) Pick pilot segment/SKU and define “first value.” Draft a 10-step onboarding checklist with owners + SLAs. Launch a no-login onboarding portal for customers. Connect CRM for auto-project creation + reminders. Ship post-kickoff and post-launch surveys. Publish weekly onboarding KPIs (TTV, DTL, capacity, activation, risk). Run two customers end-to-end; fix top bottlenecks; repeat. Why Teams Pick Onboard.io When They Decide Not to Wait Live in under a week with dynamic templates, bidirectional CRM sync, and a clean client experience. Built for scale: variables and templates that keep you flexible and consistent. Executive-ready reporting: the exact KPIs boardrooms care about. ‍ FAQ: Customer Onboarding Software What is customer onboarding software? A platform to manage post-sale implementation—tasks, owners, timelines, onboarding checklists , and customer-facing status. When should we implement it? If your TTV is slipping, DTL > target, or CSMs are juggling spreadsheets—start now with a pilot. Can we start small? Yes. Launch one onboarding template for one segment, then expand. How do we measure success? Track TTV, DTL, activation rate, go-lives per CSM , and early churn. ‍
